reason: E1 states that nanoprecipitates can improve strength-ductility synergy in HEAs but notes this approach is 'far less effective in refractory HEAs', directly contradicting the premise that it works at high temperatures. E2 supports twinning-induced toughening but only in an fcc MEA at cryogenic/room temperature, not in refractory HEAs at 600–1000 °C. E3 is unrelated to nanoprecipitates or twins. E4 shows high-temperature strength in a refractory alloy but does not mention nanoprecipitates or twins as the mechanism. Thus, the key premises lack specific prior evidence or are contradicted.
premises: Coherent nanoprecipitates in HEAs/CCAs can simultaneously strengthen and improve ductility by promoting multistage strain hardening and delaying plastic instability.
Deformation-induced nanotwinning in fcc HEAs/MEAs enhances strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at low temperatures.
The proposed hierarchical nanoprecipitate/twin network mechanism operates effectively in refractory HEAs at high temperatures (600–1000 °C).
Controlled thermomechanical processing can induce a stable network of coherent nanoprecipitates or twins in a refractory HEA/CCA.
